import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Dickson's conjecture

*References:*
- [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dickson%27s_conjecture)
- [PrimePages glossary](https://t5k.org/glossary/xpage/DicksonsConjecture.html)
- [OEIS Wiki](https://oeis.org/wiki/Dickson%27s_conjecture)
- [MathWorld](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/DicksonsConjecture.html)
- [Leonard Eugene Dickson, *History of the Theory of Numbers, Vol. I: Divisibility and Primality*](https://archive.org/details/historyoftheoryo01dickuoft)
- [Arxiv](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0906.3850)
-/
open Polynomial
namespace Dickson

/--
**Dickson's conjecture**
If a finite set of linear integer forms $f_i(n) = a_i n+b_i$ satisfies Schinzel condition,
there exist infinitely many natural numbers $m$ such that $f_i(m)$ are primes for all $i$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem dickson_conjecture (fs : Finset ℤ[X]) (hfs : ∀ f ∈ fs, f.degree = 1 ∧ BunyakovskyCondition f)
    (hfs' : SchinzelCondition fs) : Infinite {n : ℕ | ∀ f ∈ fs, (f.eval (n : ℤ)).natAbs.Prime} := by
  sorry

/-  ## Special cases -/

/--
**The generalized twin-prime conjecture**
For any positive integer $k$ there are infinitely many primes $p$ such that $p + 2k$ is prime.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem generalized_twin_primes (k : ℕ) (hk : 0 < k) :
    Infinite {p : ℕ | p.Prime ∧ (p + 2 * k).Prime} := by
  sorry

/--
**The infinitude of Sophie Germain primes**
There are infinitely many primes $p$ such that $2p + 1$ is prime.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem infinite_safe_primes :
    Infinite {p : ℕ | Prime p ∧ Prime (2 * p + 1)} := by
  sorry

/--
**The infinitude of cousin primes**
There are infinitely many primes $p$ such that $p + 4$ is prime.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem infinite_cousin_primes :
    Infinite {p : ℕ | Prime p ∧ Prime (p + 4)} := by
  sorry

/--
**The infinitude of sexy primes**
There are infinitely many primes $p$ such that $p + 6$ is prime.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem infinite_sexy_primes :
    Infinite {p : ℕ | Prime p ∧ Prime (p + 6)} := by
  sorry

/-
## Other consequences
- Landau's fourth problem (primes and perfect squares)
- Twin prime conjecture
- Artin's primitive root conjecture
- First Hardy–Littlewood conjecture

*Reference:* [Arxiv](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0906.3850)
-/

end Dickson

findings.description: The docstring at lines 35–36 mentions only the Schinzel condition and omits positive slopes. With the source's ordinary positive-prime convention, this permits a false case: {-X} satisfies SchinzelCondition, but (-X).eval n ≤ 0 for every natural n. The Lean theorem itself correctly excludes this through the positive-leading-coefficient clause of BunyakovskyCondition. Both facts about -X were checked in Lean.
findings.source_evidence: Wikipedia's opening statement explicitly requires b_i ≥ 1 in a_i + b_i n: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dickson%27s_conjecture. Zhang, arXiv:0906.3850v3, §1, likewise states f_i(x)=a_i+b_i x with b_i≥1.
findings.suggested_fix: Add “with a_i > 0” to the docstring's formulation f_i(n)=a_i n+b_i. No change to the Lean statement is needed.

findings.description: The final “Other consequences” comment, lines 82–88, attributes Landau's fourth problem to Dickson's conjecture, but the reference supplied does not support that bullet. Landau's fourth problem concerns primes n²+1, the quadratic Bunyakovsky case; it is a standard consequence of Bunyakovsky/Schinzel H, whereas the cited Dickson statement concerns linear forms. This is an unsupported consequence attribution in a comment, not a defect in any of the five Lean theorems.
findings.source_evidence: Zhang, arXiv:0906.3850v3, §1, treats f(x)=x²+1 as the simplest nonlinear Bunyakovsky case before introducing Dickson's conjecture; its subsequent list of Dickson consequences does not include Landau's fourth problem. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schinzel%27s_hypothesis_H, “Examples,” gives x²+1 as an application of H. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landau%27s_problems, “Near-square primes,” identifies the fourth problem and cites Bunyakovsky and Bateman–Horn as sufficient conjectures.
findings.suggested_fix: Remove this bullet from the Dickson consequences list, attribute it to Bunyakovsky/Schinzel H instead, or provide a reference actually establishing the claimed implication from Dickson.

reformulations.difference: The Lean uses a finset of degree-one polynomials, explicitly assumes BunyakovskyCondition, expresses admissibility by natural-number witnesses avoiding each polynomial separately, and concludes infinitude of natural inputs with prime absolute values. The source uses positive-slope linear forms, absence of a fixed divisor of their product over integer inputs, and ordinary positive prime values at positive inputs.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: A prime divides a finite product exactly when it divides a factor. Integer witnesses can be replaced by nonnegative residues modulo that prime, and any fixed divisor greater than one has a prime divisor. Admissibility forces each degree-one polynomial's coefficients to be relatively prime, implying irreducibility over ℤ; thus the additional irreducibility hypothesis is redundant. Positive slopes make every polynomial positive beyond a common finite bound, so permitting n=0 or taking natAbs changes only finitely many candidate inputs. Repetitions in an indexed family are immaterial, and the additional empty-family case is true. The scratch theorem DicksonReview.full_statement_iff proves the equivalence with a nonempty-family source formulation using positive prime values and no fixed divisor over ℤ.

reformulations.difference: The displayed set enumerates Sophie Germain primes p rather than the associated safe primes q, although the theorem name refers to safe primes. Its docstring explicitly uses the Sophie Germain formulation.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The map p ↦ 2p+1 is a bijection between primes p for which 2p+1 is prime and safe primes q, characterized by q prime and q=2p+1 for some prime p. Hence either set is infinite exactly when the other is. This was proved as DicksonReview.sophie_iff_safe. Also, Mathlib's Nat.prime_iff identifies the generic Prime predicate used here with Nat.Prime.

review.notes: No misformalization was found in any of the five Lean theorem statements; the findings concern documentation only. All recorded research-open statuses agree with the sources. The file contains no answer slots or formal_proof annotations. /workspace/review/scratch.lean compiles successfully and contains the equivalence proofs, empty/zero/constant and negative-slope checks, obstructed and admissible families, and small prime-pair computations. The equivalence proofs depend only on propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound, not the imported sorry theorems. No repository files were edited. The cited OEIS Wiki page was blocked (HTTP 403); MathWorld and the originally cited Archive item returned 404. The book was read using the alternative Archive copy listed above. PrimePages' a_i>1 wording conflicts with its own slope-one examples; Wikipedia and Zhang explicitly give the standard ≥1 restriction used by the Lean.
